title: Collections: List and Set
description: The Collection hierarchy, and the List and Set implementations: ArrayList, LinkedList, HashSet, LinkedHashSet, TreeSet.
objectives: Choose between HashSet, LinkedHashSet, and TreeSet

content.heading: The Collection Hierarchy
content.body: java.util.Collection is the root interface for group-of-objects types (excluding Map, which is a separate hierarchy since it models key-value pairs rather than a simple group). List, Set, and Queue are its main sub-interfaces. A List is an ordered collection that allows duplicates and supports indexed access (like an array, but resizable). A Set is a collection with no duplicates, modeling mathematical set semantics. Both are generic: List<String> can only hold Strings, with the compiler enforcing this at compile time.

content.heading: List and Set Implementations
content.body:
ArrayList is backed by a resizable array — fast (O(1) amortized) for indexed access and adding at the end, but O(n) for inserting/removing from the middle or beginning, since subsequent elements must shift. LinkedList is backed by a doubly-linked list — O(1) for adding/removing at either end (making it usable as a Deque too), but O(n) for indexed access, since it must traverse from an end. For most everyday use, ArrayList is the default choice; LinkedList is chosen specifically when frequent insertion/removal at the ends (not the middle by index) dominates.

HashSet offers average O(1) add/remove/contains, backed by a hash table, with no guaranteed iteration order. LinkedHashSet adds a linked structure on top, preserving insertion order during iteration at a small extra memory cost. TreeSet keeps its elements sorted (via their natural ordering, or a supplied Comparator), at O(log n) for add/remove/contains — the right choice when you need the elements in sorted order.

content.explanation: ArrayList supports get(index) directly. HashSet automatically discards the duplicate 3. TreeSet keeps its contents sorted regardless of insertion order.

keyPoints: List is ordered and allows duplicates; Set has no duplicates
ArrayList favors fast indexed access; LinkedList favors fast insertion/removal at the ends
HashSet is fastest but unordered; LinkedHashSet preserves insertion order; TreeSet keeps elements sorted
All are generic — List<String> is type-checked at compile time
commonMistakes: Defaulting to LinkedList without actually needing frequent end-insertion/removal, losing ArrayList's faster indexed access for no benefit
Expecting HashSet to preserve insertion order (it doesn't — use LinkedHashSet for that)
Adding a mutable object to a HashSet/TreeSet and then mutating it in a way that changes its hash code or ordering
